news.content: SERVING THE COMMUNITY SINCE 1977 Home India World Community Politics Economy Entertainment Legal Startups Sports Life & Style Astrology Health Opinions Classified Business SERVING THE COMMUNITY SINCE 1977 Home India World Community Politics Economy Entertainment Legal Startups Sports Life & Style Astrology Health Opinions Classified Business Home ePaper Categories India World Community Politics Economy Entertainment Legal Startups Sports Life & Style Astrology Health Opinions Classified Business About Us Contact Us Gujarat records sharp decline in malaria, dengue and chikungunya cases in 2026 Home INDIA Gujarat records sharp decline in malaria, dengue and chikungunya cases in 2026 Gujarat records sharp decline in malaria, dengue and chikungunya cases in 2026 by indiatribune August 19, 2026 2 minutes Gujarat records sharp decline in malaria, dengue and chikungunya cases in 2026 (Photo: IANS) Gandhinagar, Aug 19 (IANS) Gujarat has recorded a substantial decline in malaria, dengue and chikungunya cases this year, with the state reporting a 45 per cent fall in malaria, 39.1 per cent in dengue and 48.1 per cent in chikungunya infections up to epidemiological Week 33 compared with the corresponding period in 2025. According to data released by the Gujarat Health Department on World Mosquito Day, malaria cases fell from 1,407 in the corresponding period last year to 774 this year. In contrast, dengue cases declined from 1,293 to 788. Chikungunya cases dropped from 154 to 80. No deaths due to malaria or dengue were recorded during the period. The decline has come alongside expanded surveillance, testing, and mosquito-control measures across the state, including a house-to-house campaign that brought more than 6.51 crore people under surveillance during its second phase. The state tested more than 1.09 crore blood samples for malaria up to Week 33 of 2025, detecting 1,407 cases. In the corresponding period this year, more than 1.11 crore samples were tested, with 774 cases detected. Gujarat has also expanded diagnostic capacity for dengue and chikungunya. Diagnostic centres at 42 hospitals affiliated with medical colleges are testing for both diseases. Up to Week 33 this year, more than 83,000 serum samples for dengue and more than 12,000 for chikungunya had been tested, bringing the combined total to nearly 96,000. The state's house-to-house surveillance programme was conducted in two phases. During the first phase, from April 27 to May 6, the programme achieved 89% coverage through fever surveillance, anti-larval activities, and health education. The second phase, conducted from July 1 to 10, involved 19,558 teams and covered more than 6.51 crore people. The exercise collected more than 2.57 lakh blood samples, identifying 28 malaria patients, all of whom received treatment. The campaign has also focused on eliminating mosquito breeding grounds. House-to-house surveillance eliminated more than 29.63 lakh mosquito breeding sites, and fogging was carried out in more than 3.21 lakh houses. In malaria-sensitive areas, more than one lakh people across 116 villages in 24 districts were covered during the first round of insecticide spraying. The second round began on August 1. To strengthen field-level surveillance during the monsoon, the state deployed 497 vector-control teams across districts and municipal corporations. The teams are conducting fever surveillance and anti-larval activities in areas considered vulnerable to mosquito-borne diseases. The state has also turned to biological control measures, releasing larvivorous fish at 5,024 permanent waterlogging sites across Gujarat by the end of July. The fish target mosquito larvae at breeding sites before they develop into adult mosquitoes. "Medicines, larvicides and essential equipment had been kept adequately available, while the status of vector-borne diseases is being monitored on a daily, weekly and monthly basis," officials said. The measures come during the monsoon, when stagnant water can create breeding sites for mosquitoes. The World Health Organisation notes that many vector-borne diseases can be prevented through protective measures and community mobilisation. The measures are particularly important during the monsoon season when stagnant water can create breeding sites for mosquitoes. No deaths due to chikungunya or malaria were recorded during the period, indicating a successful containment effort.

The state reported 80 cases up to epidemiological Week 33, down from 154 in 2025. This decline is attributed to expanded surveillance, testing, and mosquito-control measures, including a house-to-house campaign that covered over 6.51 crore people in its second phase. The state tested more than 12,000 serum samples for chikungunya and has implemented various interventions such as eliminating mosquito breeding sites, fogging in over 3.21 lakh houses, and releasing larvivorous fish at 5,024 permanent waterlogging sites. Officials emphasized the availability of medicines and equipment, and the ongoing monitoring of vector-borne diseases. The measures are particularly important during the monsoon season when stagnant water can create breeding sites for mosquitoes. No deaths due to chikungunya or malaria were recorded during the period, indicating a successful containment effort.

71 chikungunya cases Steffy Thevar / Aug 23, 2026, 00:40 IST Comments Share AA +Text Size Small Medium Large Stagnant water in Khilarewadi, Erandwane Pune: PMC has reported the highest number of chikungunya cases among all civic bodies this season, according to the state health department data.Of the 1,096 chikungunya cases reported across the state between Jan 1 and Aug 21 this year, Pune Municipal Corporation (PMC) recorded 71 cases, followed by Mumbai (61), Akola (41), and Kolhapur (34). Among districts, Palghar reported the highest number with 264 cases, followed by Pune (138), Latur (56), and Dhule (55).Dr Rajesh Dighe, assistant health officer, PMC, said, “We have a robust diagnostic system at our sentinel centres, which could be one of the reasons for these higher numbers. Of the 71 reported cases, only 14 are confirmed according to central govt guidelines; the rest are suspected cases. We also have many patients arriving from neighbouring rural areas. Our records show that of the 71 patients, only 29 reside within PMC limits, 12 are from outside the city, and 32 provided incomplete addresses. Nevertheless, we have intensified action in chronic hotspots and are issuing notices to institutions found with mosquito breeding spots.”Dr Aparna Patil, district malaria officer, Pune Zilla Parishad, said, “We are focusing on diagnosing more cases because we do not want to leave any case behind. by Taboolaby Taboola Sponsored LinksSponsored Links Promoted LinksPromoted Links You May Like Brain Fog? Few Know About This Caffeine-Free Daily DrinkClear Mind Learn More Undo We are also focusing on preventive measures like releasing guppy fish into stagnant water, creating awareness, and imposing penalties on institutions found with breeding spots. Additionally, due to the high volume of migrant workers in Pune district, not all cases involve permanent Pune residents.”“Patients must monitor specific symptoms and seek immediate medical attention,” said Dr. Amit Tungenwar, consultant physician at Noble Hospitals and Research Centre. He said, “Chikungunya commonly causes prominent joint pain, often accompanied by fever and skin rashes. Dengue, on the other hand, is typically associated with high fever, severe headache, backache, pain behind the eyes, nausea, vomiting, and reduced appetite. In rare, severe cases, patients may develop bleeding from the gums, nose, or in the stool. Drowsiness, restlessness, or reduced urine output can indicate serious complications involving the brain or kidneys, requiring immediate medical intervention.”Children remain particularly vulnerable to vector-borne infections, according to Dr Nakul Pathak, consultant in paediatric intensive care and emergency at Surya Mother & Child Super Specialty Hospital. He said, “Over the past few weeks, we have witnessed a noticeable rise in both dengue and chikungunya cases due to the intermittent rains. While many patients recover with timely care, some require hospitalisation for persistent high fever, dehydration, low platelet counts, or other severe symptoms.”Dr Vineet Rao, consultant, internal medicine, Jupiter Hospital, said, “Treatment for both illnesses is mainly symptomatic, with adequate hydration and paracetamol for fever and pain forming the cornerstone of care. Early diagnosis, prompt medical attention, and the elimination of mosquito breeding sites remain the most effective measures to reduce complications. Patients should strictly avoid self-medication. The best way to stay protected is simple but consistent: avoid stagnant water around homes, use mosquito repellents and protective clothing, maintain hygiene, and seek medical advice early if a fever persists. Proper monitoring can make a huge difference in recovery.”` You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Pune | Silver Rate in Pune | Bank Holidays in Pune | Public Holidays in Pune | Petrol Price in Pune | Diesel Price in Pune | CNG Price in Pune | LPG Price in Pune Stay updated with the latest Pune news. 71 chikungunya cases Steffy Thevar / Aug 23, 2026, 00:40 IST Comments Share AA +Text Size Small Medium Large Stagnant water in Khilarewadi, Erandwane Pune: PMC has reported the highest number of chikungunya cases among all civic bodies this season, according to the state health department data.Of the 1,096 chikungunya cases reported across the state between Jan 1 and Aug 21 this year, Pune Municipal Corporation (PMC) recorded 71 cases, followed by Mumbai (61), Akola (41), and Kolhapur (34). Among districts, Palghar reported the highest number with 264 cases, followed by Pune (138), Latur (56), and Dhule (55).Dr Rajesh Dighe, assistant health officer, PMC, said, “We have a robust diagnostic system at our sentinel centres, which could be one of the reasons for these higher numbers. Of the 71 reported cases, only 14 are confirmed according to central govt guidelines; the rest are suspected cases. We also have many patients arriving from neighbouring rural areas. Our records show that of the 71 patients, only 29 reside within PMC limits, 12 are from outside the city, and 32 provided incomplete addresses. Nevertheless, we have intensified action in chronic hotspots and are issuing notices to institutions found with mosquito breeding spots.”Dr Aparna Patil, district malaria officer, Pune Zilla Parishad, said, “We are focusing on diagnosing more cases because we do not want to leave any case behind. by Taboolaby Taboola Sponsored LinksSponsored Links Promoted LinksPromoted Links You May Like Brain Fog? Few Know About This Caffeine-Free Daily DrinkClear Mind Learn More Undo We are also focusing on preventive measures like releasing guppy fish into stagnant water, creating awareness, and imposing penalties on institutions found with breeding spots. Additionally, due to the high volume of migrant workers in Pune district, not all cases involve permanent Pune residents.”“Patients must monitor specific symptoms and seek immediate medical attention,” said Dr. Amit Tungenwar, consultant physician at Noble Hospitals and Research Centre. He said, “Chikungunya commonly causes prominent joint pain, often accompanied by fever and skin rashes. Dengue, on the other hand, is typically associated with high fever, severe headache, backache, pain behind the eyes, nausea, vomiting, and reduced appetite. In rare, severe cases, patients may develop bleeding from the gums, nose, or in the stool. Drowsiness, restlessness, or reduced urine output can indicate serious complications involving the brain or kidneys, requiring immediate medical intervention.”Children remain particularly vulnerable to vector-borne infections, according to Dr Nakul Pathak, consultant in paediatric intensive care and emergency at Surya Mother & Child Super Specialty Hospital. He said, “Over the past few weeks, we have witnessed a noticeable rise in both dengue and chikungunya cases due to the intermittent rains. While many patients recover with timely care, some require hospitalisation for persistent high fever, dehydration, low platelet counts, or other severe symptoms.”Dr Vineet Rao, consultant, internal medicine, Jupiter Hospital, said, “Treatment for both illnesses is mainly symptomatic, with adequate hydration and paracetamol for fever and pain forming the cornerstone of care. Early diagnosis, prompt medical attention, and the elimination of mosquito breeding sites remain the most effective measures to reduce complications. Patients should strictly avoid self-medication. The best way to stay protected is simple but consistent: avoid stagnant water around homes, use mosquito repellents and protective clothing, maintain hygiene, and seek medical advice early if a fever persists. news.content: TODAY’S PAPER | August 25, 2026 | EPAPER ☰ Home Latest Pakistan Business World Sports Opinion Life & Style T-Magazine Blogs Tech Cartoon Home World Global warming ‘expands spread’ of TBE, chikungunya Rising mercury takes tick and mosquito-borne diseases to new regions REUTERS August 22, 2026 1 min read facebook twitter whatsup linkded email GDANSK: Global warming is expanding the geographical spread of tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) and chikungunya, with warmer temperatures and milder winters helping disease-carrying ticks and mosquitoes move into new regions, the chief executive of vaccine maker Bavarian Nordic said on Friday. Advertisement X Paul Chaplin said Germany was among the countries already experiencing the impact, with the number of regions considered at risk of TBE increasing year after year. “The number of regions in Germany that are now considered to be at risk of TBE increases year after year,” Chaplin told Reuters. Chaplin noted that the disease was moving north from its traditional stronghold in southern Germany. He added TBE was also increasing in Scandinavia as warmer temperatures and milder winters allowed tick populations to grow and expand their range. Germany reported 693 TBE cases last year, the third-highest annual figure since data collection began in 2001, according to the Robert Koch Institute. Chaplin said chikungunya, a mosquito-borne disease typically found in Asia and South America, was also moving into Europe and the United States. Mosquitoes capable of transmitting the virus are already present in Europe, meaning imported cases can trigger local outbreaks, he said, pointing to previous outbreaks in Italy and France. France has reported locally acquired chikungunya cases this year. According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) ambient temperature is among the most important environmental factors influencing the transmission of chikungunya. facebook news.title_original: Global warming ‘expands spread’ of TBE, chikungunya - The Express Tribune

analysis.time: Global warming is expanding the geographical spread of tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) and chikungunya, with warmer temperatures and milder winters helping disease-carrying ticks and mosquitoes move into new regions, the chief executive of vaccine maker Bavarian Nordic said on Friday. Germany reported 693 TBE cases last year, the third-highest annual figure since data collection began in 2001, according to the Robert Koch Institute. France has reported locally acquired chikungunya cases this year.
analysis.location_and_population: Germany and France are among the countries experiencing the impact of global warming on the spread of TBE and chikungunya. The Robert Koch Institute reported TBE cases in Germany, while France has reported locally acquired chikungunya cases. The ECDC highlighted the influence of ambient temperature on chikungunya transmission.
analysis.event: The chief executive of vaccine maker Bavarian Nordic, Paul Chaplin, stated that warmer temperatures and milder winters are enabling disease-carrying ticks and mosquitoes to move into new regions. Germany has seen an increase in TBE cases, and France has reported locally acquired chikungunya cases.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The ECDC noted that ambient temperature is a key environmental factor influencing chikungunya transmission. TBE is also increasing in Scandinavia due to expanding tick populations.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The spread of TBE and chikungunya is being discussed by experts, with Paul Chaplin noting the northward movement of TBE from southern Germany and the potential for local outbreaks in Europe due to existing mosquito populations. The ECDC has identified ambient temperature as a critical factor in chikungunya transmission. These findings are based on reported data and expert analysis, with no indication of a specific response or containment strategy.

analysis.brief_en: Global warming is expanding the spread of tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) and chikungunya, according to Paul Chaplin, CEO of Bavarian Nordic. Warmer temperatures and milder winters are enabling ticks and mosquitoes to move into new regions, increasing the risk of TBE in Germany and chikungunya in Europe and the United States. Germany reported 693 TBE cases in 2025, the third-highest since data collection began in 2001, while France has seen locally acquired chikungunya cases this year. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) highlighted that ambient temperature is a key factor in chikungunya transmission. Chaplin also noted that chikungunya, typically found in Asia and South America, is moving into Europe, with imported cases potentially triggering local outbreaks. These findings are based on expert analysis and reported data, with no specific containment strategy mentioned.

Germany reported 693 TBE cases in 2025, the third-highest since data collection began in 2001, while France has seen locally acquired chikungunya cases this year. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) highlighted that ambient temperature is a key factor in chikungunya transmission. Chaplin also noted that chikungunya, typically found in Asia and South America, is moving into Europe, with imported cases potentially triggering local outbreaks. These findings are based on expert analysis and reported data, with no specific containment strategy mentioned.

elements_zh.time: 全球变暖正在扩大蜱传脑炎(TBE)与基孔肯雅热的地理传播范围,气温升高与冬季变暖使携带病原体的蜱虫与蚊虫得以进入新的地区,巴伐利亚北方公司(该公司生产疫苗)首席执行官保罗·查普林于周五表示。据罗伯特·科赫研究所数据,德国去年报告了693例蜱传脑炎病例,为2001年数据收集以来的第三高发年份。法国今年已报告本地获得性基孔肯雅热病例。
elements_zh.location_and_population: 德国与法国是受全球变暖影响、蜱传脑炎与基孔肯雅热传播扩散的国家之一。罗伯特·科赫研究所报告了德国的蜱传脑炎病例,而法国报告了本地获得性基孔肯雅热病例。欧洲疾病预防与控制中心(ECDC)强调了环境温度对基孔肯雅热传播的影响。
elements_zh.event: 巴伐利亚北方公司(该公司生产疫苗)首席执行官保罗·查普林表示,气温升高与冬季变暖使携带病原体的蜱虫与蚊虫得以进入新的地区。德国蜱传脑炎病例有所增加,法国报告了本地获得性基孔肯雅热病例。
elements_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 欧洲疾病预防与控制中心(ECDC)指出,环境温度是影响基孔肯雅热传播的关键环境因素。蜱传脑炎(TBE)也因蜱虫种群扩张而在斯堪的纳维亚地区呈上升趋势。
elements_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 蜱传脑炎与基孔肯雅热的传播正由专家讨论,保罗·查普林指出蜱传脑炎正从德国南部向北扩散,且欧洲现有蚊虫种群可能引发当地暴发。欧洲疾病预防与控制中心(ECDC)已将环境温度识别为影响基孔肯雅热传播的关键因素。上述发现基于报告数据与专家分析,未显示出具体的应对或防控策略。

news.content: Skip to main content News Radio Events Newsletter Giveaway Contact Home Radio Home Schedule Home Contact Home Advertise with us Our Advertisers Skip to main content News Radio Events Newsletter Giveaway Contact On Air Now Listen Now Fia Tarrant 7pm - 10pm7pm to 10pm Mosquito crackdown as chikungunya cases rise in south-west France Mosquito control is being stepped up in south-west France after more than 20 locally acquired cases of chikungunya were reported. 20 Aug 2026, 08:09 | Updated: 4d ago Share Link Copied Mosquito crackdown as chikungunya cases rise in south-west France. Picture: Alamy By Camille Bidard Mosquito control operations are being stepped up across parts of south-west France after more than 20 locally acquired cases of chikungunya were identified. Listen to this article Loading audio... The outbreaks are mainly concentrated in Gironde and Tarn, with cases also reported near Toulouse. In Prignac-et-Marcamps, north of Bordeaux, 16 cases have been recorded in a population of around 1,500. Authorities have launched insect-control operations and are asking residents to remove standing water where tiger mosquitoes breed. Some outdoor sports activities have also been suspended in the affected commune. The Asian tiger mosquito is now established in 83 mainland French departments, allowing diseases normally associated with tropical regions to spread locally. Chikungunya is rarely life-threatening but can cause sudden fever, severe joint and muscle pain, headaches, fatigue and rashes. Joint pain can sometimes persist for weeks or months. Residents in affected areas are advised to wear long clothing, use mosquito repellent, cover water containers and regularly empty anything that can collect stagnant water. The tiger mosquito is particularly active during the daytime, especially in the morning and late afternoon

Updated: Fri 21 Aug 2026 12:09 CET Share Add a comment Asian tiger mosquitoes can spread potentially serious illnesses including chikungunya and dengue fever. Photo by Martin LELIEVRE / AFP Cases of the tropical diseases of chikungunya and dengue fever have been reported in south-west France, including Dordogne, thought to be spread by tiger mosquitoes. Diseases like chikungunya, dengue and West Nile fever are usually found in people who have visited tropical regions where the illnesses are endemic - but France is seeing an increasing number of cases among people who have no recent travel history. It is believed that the illnesses are being spread by tiger mosquitoes, which have been gradually spreading through France in recent years, due to warming temperatures. The most recent bulletin from Santé Publique France records several cases of transmission autochtone (local transmission) in the Nouvelle Aquitaine region. In the August 18th bulletin, three cases of locally transmitted chikungunya were reported in the Gironde département, which includes Bordeaux, while one case of dengue fever was reported in Dordogne. In Gironde, cases were reported in Saint-Médard-en-Jalles and Prignac-et-Marcamps, while a third case in Talence is believed to be linked to the Prignac-et-Marcamps case. These reports cover only those who went to the doctor and were diagnosed with the illness - in many people the symptoms are mild and may not have required a doctor visit. Advertisement In Dordogne, the dengue fever case was reported in Mouleydier, near Bergerac. Local transmission still accounts for a minority of cases - most of the recorded cases are among those who have recently returned from regions in Africa or Asia where the diseases are endemic. Santé Publique France added that over the course of the summer, 28 cases of travel-related chikungunya were reported in the Nouvelle Aquitaine region, and 18 dengue cases. Local transmission of the illnesses has been linked to tiger mosquitoes - originally from Asia, the mosquitoes have been gradually spreading north through Europe over the last decade, as warming temperatures make the environment more attractive to them. READ ALSO: MAP: Where tiger mosquitoes are found in France Santé Publique France recorded several local mosquito-killing operations after reports of chikungunya and dengue. These illnesses can be serious, but fatalities are very rare in patients who have access to good medical care. Chikungunya - According to French health authorities, in approximately 10 to 40 percent of cases, chikungunya is asymptomatic. Symptoms include a sudden onset of high fever, joint pain that can be intense, muscle pain, headache, and a rash. For most people, the illness runs its course in 10 days with no aftereffects, but in 30 to 40 percent of patients who experience symptoms, it can lead to persistent joint pain. Dengue fever - It is asymptomatic in 50 to 90 percent of cases. For those who are symptomatic, the incubation period on average lasts four to seven days, but it can be three to 14 days, according to Santé Publique France. The 'classic' form involves a high fever, chills, headache, 'retro-orbital' (behind the eyes) pain, vomiting, joint and muscle pain, and occasionally a rash around the fifth day of symptoms. Most of the time, the illness goes away after a few days. However, one to five percent of symptomatic cases can become severe and life-threatening. news.content: Home News Policy Public Health Digitisation Startup People Interview Opinion Appointment Drug Approval Supply Chain Packaging Biotech Sustainability Events Upcoming Events Past Events Healthcare Hospitals Diagnostic Center Equipment White Papers Home » Healthcare » Doctors urge vigilance against Dengue, Malaria and Chikungunya during monsoon Healthcare Doctors urge vigilance against Dengue, Malaria and Chikungunya during monsoon CARE Hospitals experts highlight that a fall in fever does not necessarily indicate recovery in dengue and stress the importance of timely clinical assessment, appropriate investigations, hydration and monitoring. By IPP Bureau | August 19, 2026 With the monsoon driving a rise in fever cases, doctors at CARE Hospitals have urged people not to dismiss persistent fever and body aches as a routine viral infection, warning that delayed diagnosis of dengue, malaria and chikungunya can increase the risk of complications. According to the National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC), India reported 2,33,519 dengue cases and 297 deaths in 2024, while Telangana recorded 10,077 cases. Dr. Syed Mustafa Ashraf, Senior General Physician, CARE Hospitals, Malakpet, said dengue, malaria and chikungunya can initially present with symptoms similar to viral fever. Persistent fever, worsening weakness, repeated vomiting, severe abdominal pain, unusual bleeding, drowsiness, breathing difficulty or reduced urine output should prompt medical evaluation. Doctors also highlighted that a fall in fever does not necessarily indicate recovery in dengue and stressed the importance of timely clinical assessment, appropriate investigations, hydration and monitoring. Dr. Chaitanya Challa, Senior Consultant – General Medicine, CARE Hospitals, Banjara Hills, said mosquito-borne disease prevention should continue beyond the monsoon. In urban areas, mosquitoes can breed in small amounts of stagnant water found in coolers, flowerpot trays, buckets, tyres, discarded containers, construction sites and uncovered tanks. Doctors recommended inspecting homes and surroundings at least once a week, removing stagnant water, keeping water-storage containers covered and using mosquito repellents, protective clothing and window and door screens. Since Aedesmosquitoes, which transmit dengue, are primarily active during the daytime, daytime protection is also important. Ahead of World Mosquito Day on August 20, CARE Hospitals doctors called for greater awareness of warning signs and cautioned against indiscriminate self-medication for fever, emphasising that mosquito prevention should remain a year-round practice rather than a seasonal exercise. Dr. Syed Mustafa Ashraf, Senior General Physician, CARE Hospitals, Malakpet, said dengue, malaria and chikungunya can initially present with symptoms similar to viral fever. Persistent fever, worsening weakness, repeated vomiting, severe abdominal pain, unusual bleeding, drowsiness, breathing difficulty or reduced urine output should prompt medical evaluation. Doctors also highlighted that a fall in fever does not necessarily indicate recovery in dengue and stressed the importance of timely clinical assessment, appropriate investigations, hydration and monitoring. Dr. Chaitanya Challa, Senior Consultant – General Medicine, CARE Hospitals, Banjara Hills, said mosquito-borne disease prevention should continue beyond the monsoon. In urban areas, mosquitoes can breed in small amounts of stagnant water found in coolers, flowerpot trays, buckets, tyres, discarded containers, construction sites and uncovered tanks. Doctors recommended inspecting homes and surroundings at least once a week, removing stagnant water, keeping water-storage containers covered and using mosquito repellents, protective clothing and window and door screens. Since Aedesmosquitoes, which transmit dengue, are primarily active during the daytime, daytime protection is also important. Ahead of World Mosquito Day on August 20, CARE Hospitals doctors called for greater awareness of warning signs and cautioned against indiscriminate self-medication for fever, emphasising that mosquito prevention should remain a year-round practice rather than a seasonal exercise. Source: ECDC/EFSA Stockholm, 20 August 2026 Europe needs to improve its preparedness and control efforts as the risk of mosquito-borne diseases increases, with West Nile virus (WNV) continuing to spread to new regions and invasive mosquito species becoming established in more parts of Europe, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said on World Mosquito Day. This year, six regions in Europe reported locally acquired infections with WNV for the first time ever. According to ECDC’s most recent weekly figures, 429 locally acquired cases of WNV infection have been reported in nine European countries as of 13 August 2026. As transmission usually peaks during August and early September, further cases can be expected. ‘The expansion of West Nile virus transmission as well as the spread of invasive mosquito species demonstrate why Europe needs to strengthen its mosquito-control capacity,’ says Céline Gossner of ECDC. ‘For effective mosquito control, we need close cooperation in Europe and an integrated approach that brings together mosquito monitoring, community engagement, and targeted mosquito control solutions that take environmental impact into account.’ While the mosquitoes that spread WNV (Culex mosquitoes) are already widely present in Europe, the Asian tiger mosquito (Aedes albopictus), which can transmit dengue and chikungunya viruses, is now established in 16 European countries, double the number from 12 years ago. A new article published today by ECDC and EU partners in the Eurosurveillance journal, ‘Strengthening mosquito control to manage emerging mosquito-borne diseases’, identifies gaps in Europe’s mosquito-control capacity and calls for improved coordination and a bigger toolbox to increase mosquito control. This coincides with the publication of a new ECDC report on mosquito surveillance and control practices in Europe, highlighting the need for more effective mosquito-control programmes. ECDC works to support European countries through seasonal surveillance of WNV infections, dengue and chikungunya virus disease, alongside risk assessments, mosquito-distribution maps, modelling and practical guidance on preparedness, prevention and outbreak response. Effective mosquito control requires an integrated approach that combines mosquito and disease surveillance, larval source management, community engagement, and targeted mosquito control adapted to local conditions. Insecticide resistance, environmental concerns, and the limited range of products authorised for use against mosquitoes also underline the need for more diversified control options and stronger evidence on their effectiveness, safety, and environmental impact. By removing or covering stagnant water in and around homes, including balconies and gardens, communities and individuals have an important role to play in helping to reduce mosquito populations. Personal protection is also important, including using repellents, wearing protective clothing and mosquito-proofing homes. Healthcare professionals should also remain alert to local transmission and the possibility of importation to prevent the further spread of these viruses. news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Monday, August 24, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health World Mosquito Day 2026: EU scientists urge mosquito control as diseases rise by Bioengineer August 21, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Mosquito control must become a stronger and more coordinated public-health priority as dengue, chikungunya and West Nile virus infection become increasingly established risks in Europe, according to scientists from the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA), the European Environment Agency (EEA) and the European Commission. In a commentary published in Eurosurveillance on 20 August 2026, the authors argue that Europe needs sustainable, evidence-based and integrated strategies to manage mosquito populations and reduce the probability that infectious diseases will spread. Their assessment, published on World Mosquito Day, links the changing epidemiology of mosquito-borne disease to a combination of environmental transformation, climate change and increased international movement of people. Mosquitoes are biological vectors: they acquire viruses when feeding on an infected host and can later transmit those viruses through subsequent bites. The capacity of a mosquito population to sustain transmission depends on several interacting factors, including the presence of competent mosquito species, temperature, rainfall, breeding habitats, virus introduction and the availability of humans or animals that can serve as hosts. Warmer conditions can accelerate viral replication inside mosquitoes and shorten the time required for them to become infectious, while changes in rainfall and water management can create new larval habitats. More frequent international travel can also introduce viruses into areas where mosquito populations are present but local transmission has previously been limited or absent. Discover more infections Pest Control infection Health The European disease landscape has already demonstrated why this issue requires sustained attention. Aedes mosquitoes, which can transmit dengue and chikungunya viruses, have expanded their presence in parts of Europe, while Culex mosquitoes are important vectors of West Nile virus. The establishment of a vector does not automatically lead to an outbreak, because transmission also depends on virus circulation, weather, human behaviour and public-health preparedness. Nevertheless, when suitable mosquitoes and favourable environmental conditions coincide, imported infections can lead to local transmission. The authors therefore describe mosquito control as an essential component of outbreak prevention rather than merely a response used after disease transmission has begun. The most direct way to reduce mosquito abundance is to eliminate or manage the stagnant water in which larvae develop. Containers, rainwater collection points, blocked drainage systems and other small pools can provide breeding sites for Aedes mosquitoes, while larger wetlands, irrigation structures and urban water systems may support other species. Where water cannot be removed, larvicides can be used to target immature mosquitoes before they emerge as adults capable of biting and transmitting pathogens. During outbreaks, adult mosquitoes may also be targeted with biocidal products. These interventions can reduce vector density rapidly, but their performance depends on local ecology, timing, coverage, application methods and repeated monitoring. Another approach now being piloted in Europe is the sterile insect technique, or SIT. This method involves mass-rearing male mosquitoes, sterilising them and releasing them into areas where they can mate with wild females. Because the resulting eggs are infertile, repeated releases can reduce the reproductive capacity of the target population. Male mosquitoes do not bite, so the technique is designed to suppress populations without increasing the number of biting insects. SIT may offer a valuable alternative or complement to chemical control, but its effectiveness depends on accurate releases, adequate population coverage and detailed knowledge of mosquito ecology. It also requires assessment of operational costs, long-term sustainability and effects under different environmental conditions. Discover more Infectious Diseases health Insects & Entomology Chemical control remains important, yet it presents a growing scientific and regulatory challenge. Pyrethroids account for most of the substances approved for adult mosquito control and can interfere with the normal function of insect nervous systems, producing rapid knockdown or death. Their extensive use, however, raises concerns about possible effects on human health and non-target organisms, particularly when applications become broader or more frequent. Mosquito resistance is an additional threat. Genetic changes affecting insecticide target sites, increased detoxification of active compounds or behavioural changes can allow mosquitoes to survive exposure. As resistance increases, products may become less effective, forcing programmes to improve surveillance, rotate control methods and avoid unnecessary applications. The commentary identifies major gaps in the evidence needed to decide which interventions should be used, where and at what scale. Reliable comparisons of cost-effectiveness remain limited, especially for programmes that combine larval control, adult control, environmental management, personal protection and emerging technologies. A measure that works in one setting may perform poorly elsewhere because mosquito species, housing, infrastructure, climate and community behaviour differ. Countries also vary in the biocidal products they approve and in the rules governing their use. These differences can complicate cross-border responses, procurement and the rapid deployment of control measures when vectors or viruses move across national boundaries. Personal protection remains an important layer of prevention, even when public authorities are operating mosquito-control programmes. Repellents can reduce the likelihood of bites, while long clothing, window and door screens, and mosquito nets can create physical barriers between people and vectors. Such measures are particularly important for individuals infected with a mosquito-borne virus, because preventing additional bites can reduce the opportunity for mosquitoes to acquire the virus and pass it to others. Personal protection cannot replace population-level control, but it can reduce exposure while surveillance teams investigate transmission and authorities apply targeted interventions. The authors argue that fragmented governance is one of the greatest obstacles to effective mosquito control. Responsibility commonly rests with ministries of health, although municipal authorities may lead local operations, and ministries responsible for agriculture, the environment, transport or urban development may also influence mosquito habitats and disease risk. Control plans are frequently designed below the national level and implemented by private contractors, creating potential differences in capacity and performance. ECDC surveys conducted in 2020 and 2025 found that 20 of 29 countries reported active mosquito-control measures, with most focusing on larvae. However, the absence of a political perception that mosquito-borne diseases represent an immediate priority can limit investment in surveillance, laboratory capacity, trained personnel and long-term prevention. At the European level, the response involves institutions with different but complementary responsibilities. ECDC and the European Food Safety Authority provide scientific guidance and surveillance expertise for human and animal health, while ECHA evaluates biocidal substances and products used for mosquito control. The EEA contributes environmental and climate information that can help identify changing conditions and assess risk, and the European Commission supports the implementation of health legislation, vector surveillance, public-health measures, coordination and research funding. The scientists call for these activities to be connected through a One Health framework that includes public health, veterinary medicine, environmental protection and urban planning. By combining information on human cases, animal infections, mosquito abundance, insecticide resistance, climate and land use, Europe could detect emerging risks earlier and select interventions that reduce disease transmission while protecting ecosystems and communities. news.title_zh: 2026年世界蚊子日:欧盟科学家敦促加强蚊虫控制,应对疾病上升趋势 - Bioengineer.org
news.source_body_en: On August 21, 2026, EU scientists from the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA), the European Environment Agency (EEA), and the European Commission urged stronger mosquito control measures as mosquito-borne diseases like chikungunya, dengue, and West Nile virus become increasingly established risks in Europe. The commentary, published in Eurosurveillance on August 20, 2026, links the spread of these diseases to environmental changes, climate change, and increased international travel. It emphasizes the need for sustainable, evidence-based strategies to manage mosquito populations and reduce disease transmission. The article highlights that while mosquito control is essential, its effectiveness depends on local ecology, timing, coverage, and repeated monitoring. It also notes the challenges of fragmented governance and the importance of cross-border coordination. The authors stress that personal protection measures, such as repellents and mosquito nets, remain important even when public authorities implement control programs.
news.content_zh: 2026年8月21日,来自欧洲疾病预防控制中心(ECDC)、欧洲化学品管理局(ECHA)、欧洲环境署(EEA)及欧盟委员会的欧盟科学家敦促加强蚊虫控制措施,因包括基孔肯雅热、登革热和西尼罗河病毒病在内的蚊媒疾病在欧洲已成为日益严峻的风险。该评论文章于2026年8月20日发表在《欧洲监测》期刊上,将这些疾病的传播与环境变化、气候变化及国际旅行增加联系起来。文章强调需采用可持续的、循证策略来控制蚊虫种群并降低疾病传播风险。文章指出,蚊虫控制固然重要,但其有效性取决于当地生态环境、实施时机、覆盖范围及重复监测。同时,文章还指出碎片化治理带来的挑战,并强调跨境协调的重要性。作者强调,即使公共当局实施控制计划,个人防护措施(如驱蚊剂和蚊帐)仍然重要。

news.content_title: Dr Anelia Zasheva tells FAKTI: The presence of tiger mosquitoes in our country does not mean that they are infected
news.content: Mosquitoes are not just an annoying summer problem. They can be carriers of serious infections, some of which are already appearing in Europe under conditions that were previously less common. West Nile fever deserves special attention, since a large part of those infected have no symptoms and may not even realize that they have had the infection. Against the backdrop of higher temperatures, longer warm seasons and the spread of the Asian tiger mosquito in Bulgaria, prevention is becoming increasingly important. What are the real risks, which symptoms should not be underestimated and how can we protect ourselves from diseases transmitted by mosquitoes... Dr. Anelia Zasheva, an infectious diseases specialist at the Military Medical Academy, spoke to FACTI. - Dr. Zasheva, what are the most dangerous infections that can be transmitted through a mosquito bite, and which of them pose a real risk to people in Bulgaria? - When we talk about the “most dangerous” infections, it is necessary to distinguish the global burden of diseases from the real risk to Bulgaria. Worldwide, malaria remains the leading cause of mortality among mosquito-borne infections. Yellow fever, severe dengue, which usually develops with repeated illness, Japanese encephalitis and the neuroinvasive form of West Nile infection can be particularly serious and life-threatening. Chikungunya is rarely fatal, but it can cause prolonged and severe joint pain, and Zika infection is particularly dangerous during pregnancy due to the risks to the fetus. The immediate risk for people in Bulgaria is West Nile infection. Its main vectors are mosquitoes of the genus Culex, and the virus circulates between mosquitoes and birds. Malaria, dengue, chikungunya and Zika are currently mainly associated with travel. The establishment of the Asian tiger mosquito creates the possibility of an imported virus being transmitted locally, but this is a potential risk. - West Nile fever is among the diseases that are already occurring in our country. Why do about 80% of infected people have no symptoms and how does this make it difficult to detect the infection? - There is no single reason why one person remains asymptomatic and another becomes ill. The clinical outcome depends on the interaction between the virus and the body – age, immune response, concomitant diseases, individual genetic characteristics, viral strain and probably the amount of virus at the time of infection. In most people, the immune system limits the multiplication of the virus before a clinically apparent disease develops. According to various epidemiological and clinical studies, about 20% of people develop symptoms such as fever, headache, fatigue, muscle pain, sometimes rash, nausea or enlarged lymph nodes. These symptoms are non-specific and can easily be attributed to another viral infection, especially in the summer season. Therefore, the registered cases do not represent the total spread of the infection. The real circulation is estimated not only by diagnosed patients, but also by examining blood donors, mosquitoes, birds and horses. - What are the first symptoms that should make us seek medical help after a mosquito bite – especially if we have been abroad or in an area with established circulation of the infection? - It is not necessary to seek medical attention after every bite. The usual redness, itching and slight swelling are a local reaction to the mosquito's saliva and most often pass without complications. A medical consultation is necessary if in the following days or weeks a fever, severe headache, severe fatigue, muscle or joint pain, pain behind the eyes, rash, nausea or vomiting occur. Immediate help should be sought in case of confusion, drowsiness, neck stiffness, seizures, sudden muscle weakness or paralysis, difficulty breathing, persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, bleeding or fainting. A particularly important rule is that any fever during or after traveling to an area with malaria should be evaluated urgently - even if the person has taken prophylaxis. The doctor should be informed exactly where, when and for how long the patient has traveled, as well as what prophylaxis he has taken. If dengue is suspected, aspirin and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs should not be taken arbitrarily until the diagnosis has been ruled out, as they can increase the risk of bleeding. - How serious can the complications of West Nile infection be and which people are most at risk of severe nervous system damage? - Approximately one in 150 infected people develops neuroinvasive disease - meningitis, encephalitis or involvement of the anterior horns of the spinal cord, which can resemble poliomyelitis and cause acute flaccid paralysis. In the most severe cases, the respiratory muscles may also be affected. It is important to note that the severe form is rare compared to all diagnosed cases, but when it develops, it can be life-threatening. Among patients with neuroinvasive disease, the mortality rate in some studies and seasons reaches 20%, and some of those who have recovered may have prolonged weakness, memory and concentration disorders, tremors or other neurological consequences. The risk increases with age, especially in people over 60-65 years of age. People with a suppressed immune system, transplant patients and patients with oncological diseases, diabetes, chronic kidney disease or arterial hypertension are particularly at risk. However, severe cases have also been recorded in young people. There is still no approved vaccine or specific antiviral treatment. - The Asian tiger mosquito already has established populations in Bulgaria. How can we recognize it and does its presence mean that there is already a real risk of dengue, chikungunya and Zika in our country? - The Asian tiger mosquito – Aedes albopictus – is relatively small and dark. It has clearly defined white or silvery rings on its legs and a single light longitudinal line on the upper side of the thorax. Unlike many common mosquitoes, it bites aggressively mainly during the day, most often outdoors. However, a photo alone cannot always reliably distinguish it from other similar species. Observations can also be submitted through the NCCSPB Mosquito Alert project. Its presence is a necessary, but not sufficient condition for the local spread of dengue, chikungunya or Zika. It takes an infected traveler to arrive in Bulgaria while the virus is circulating in their bloodstream; a local mosquito to bite them; the temperature to allow the virus to multiply in the mosquito; and then the same mosquito to bite another person. Therefore, the risk is possible, but it depends on many factors. The presence of tiger mosquitoes in our country does not mean that they are infected or that these diseases are already endemic. Local outbreaks of dengue and chikungunya in other European countries show that such a chain of transmission is possible. For Zika, Aedes albopictus is considered a less efficient vector compared to Aedes aegypti. - How climate change – higher temperatures, longer summers and milder winters – change the spread of mosquitoes and the infections they carry? - Higher temperatures accelerate the development of mosquitoes and, under the right conditions, shorten the time it takes for the virus to become infectious in the mosquito itself. Longer summers extend the transmission season, and milder winters facilitate the survival of eggs and the establishment of invasive species. Precipitation also matters. Rain creates water habitats, but periods of drought can also increase the risk when people start storing water in open containers. The relationship is not completely linear - extreme heat and prolonged drought can also reduce some populations. - Could Bulgaria become a more suitable environment for these diseases? - Bulgaria can become, and to some extent has already become, more suitable for certain mosquitoes and infections. This is evidenced by the establishment of the tiger mosquito and the periodic circulation of the West Nile virus. But climate is not the only factor. International travel, urbanization, water management, vector surveillance and timely control also determine whether an outbreak will occur. Therefore, a more favorable environment does not mean that Bulgaria will inevitably become a tropical endemic zone. - What should people who travel to countries with widespread malaria, dengue, yellow fever or other infections know? When is a vaccine needed, and when is drug prophylaxis needed? - It is best to consult with an infectious disease specialist four to eight weeks before departure. Not only the country is evaluated, but also the specific region, season, altitude, duration and mode of travel, as well as the age, presence of pregnancy, concomitant diseases and immune status of the traveler. Even when traveling at the last minute, consultation makes sense. A vaccine is used for yellow fever, which is recommended for some countries, and for others the certificate is a condition for entry. One dose provides long-lasting, usually lifelong protection, but the vaccine has contraindications and requires individual assessment, especially in immunosuppressed, pregnant women, young children and people over 60 years of age. For travelers to malarial areas, the main specific method is drug prophylaxis. The choice between the different drugs depends on local resistance, contraindications and the route. They are started before the trip and continued during the stay and a certain period after return, which varies for the individual drugs. There is no drug prophylaxis for dengue. There is a vaccine, but it is not a universal recommendation for every tourist and its use depends on age, data on previous infection, length of stay and current national recommendations. Neither the vaccine nor drug prophylaxis replaces protection from bites: repellent, covering clothing, nets, air-conditioned rooms and appropriately treated nets or clothing. - Can we distinguish a simple mosquito bite from a situation in which we are likely to be infected with a virus or parasite? And does it make sense for a person to test their blood prophylactically after a bite? - No. An infected mosquito does not look different, and the bite itself does not indicate whether the pathogen has been transmitted. Itching, redness and swelling are a reaction to the mosquito's saliva, not to the virus or parasite. Prophylactic testing after a single bite in a person without symptoms usually has no medical meaning. If done too early, the test may be negative despite the infection having occurred. On the other hand, some antibody tests may cross-react with other similar viruses or indicate an old, rather than a current infection. Tests are ordered when there is a combination of symptoms, an appropriate incubation period, and actual epidemiological exposure. Exceptions may include special recommendations for pregnant women after possible Zika exposure, measures for blood donation, or specific instructions from health authorities. - What are the most effective measures to limit mosquitoes around our homes? How important is it to remove stagnant water and why can even small containers become mosquito breeding grounds? - Removing stagnant water is one of the most effective measures, especially against the tiger mosquito. Once a week, we should empty, wash and scrub or turn over all containers that can hold water: pot bases, buckets, watering cans, children's toys, vases, tires, gutters, covers, birdbaths and pet bowls. It is important not only to pour out the water, but also to scrub the walls. The tiger mosquito lays desiccation-resistant eggs just above the waterline, and these can remain attached to the container until it is flooded again. The larvae do not need a swamp for development - a small amount of water in a forgotten container is enough. Rainwater tanks should be tightly covered, pools - properly maintained, and window and door screens - strong. When water cannot be removed, only approved larvicides can be used and exactly as directed. Spraying against adult mosquitoes has a temporary effect and cannot replace the removal of breeding sites. - What is the most important message to people during the summer season – what should we really be afraid of and what can we do to reduce the risk of infections without becoming unnecessarily anxious? - We should not be afraid of every bite. For the vast majority of people, it will only cause short-term itching and redness. But we should not underestimate the fact that conditions in Europe are changing and some mosquito-borne infections are now a real, albeit relatively rare, possibility. The most sensible approach is to be informed without panicking: to use repellent and appropriate clothing, to limit areas with stagnant water and to put nets on windows. If you have a fever or unusual symptoms after traveling, you should seek medical attention and always report where you were and for how long. It is not the mosquito itself that should scare us, but the ignored fever after a risky trip, the missed warning symptoms, and the lack of basic prevention. Most risks can be minimized with a few consistent and completely doable habits

news.content: Skip to main content Login Register News Magazines An Interactive Experience Current Issue August 2026 View this Issue Archive Quarterly Magazine Current Issue June 2026 View this Issue ArchiveFeatures Topics Life Sciences Biochemistry Cancer Cell & Molecular Biology Developmental Biology Evolutionary Biology Genetics Genome Editing Immunology Microbiology Neuroscience Omics Physiology Health & Medicine Cell & Gene Therapy Diagnostics Drug Discovery & Development Public Health Science & Society Community Careers Research Ethics Science Communication Biotechnology Artificial Intelligence Business Laboratory Technology Synthetic Biology Resources Crossword Puzzles eBooks Infographics Innovation Spotlight Podcasts Product Coverage Research Product Blog Industry Articles Videos Words for Nerds Webinars Register Home/ Categories/ Life Sciences/ Microbiology Article How Wolbachia Emerged as an Ally in the Fight Against Disease Vectors From blocking viral replication to suppressing pathogenic worms, Wolbachia’s unusual relationships with its hosts inspire new ways to control disease spread. Brought to you byThe Scientist Aug 24, 2026 | 4 min read Save for Later Researchers leverage Wolbachia to combat mosquito-borne viruses, target parasitic worms, and engage citizen scientists. Image credit:© iStock.com, iiievgeniy PDF version Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 4:00 Discovered more than a century ago in mosquitoes, the bacterial genus Wolbachia is one of the most common parasitic microbes of insects. The bacteria reside in the cytoplasm of host cells and modify their reproductive capabilities, often resulting in sterility. Over the past 100 years, this endosymbiont has captivated researchers’ interest, both due to its interaction with its host and because of its applications in controlling disease vectors. Dive in to revisit the endosymbiont’s journey, right from its discovery to how researchers leverage it to control vector-borne viruses like dengue, target the obligate bacteria inside parasitic filarial worms, and engage citizen scientists globally to map its vast biological distribution. A Century of Wolbachia: From Discovery to Controlling Diseases In the early 1900s, entomologist Marshall Hertig and pathologist Simeon Burt Wolbach brought mosquitoes to their lab to characterize the microbes they harbored. Dissecting insect tissues and examining them under the microscope revealed bacteria in their ovaries, testes, and eggs. Over time, the researchers found these endosymbionts in a number of insect species and identified that infected female insects passed Wolbachia to their offspring. Digging deeper, researchers discovered that Wolbachia manipulated its host reproductive success, turning the bacterium into an unlikely ally in the fight against pathogens. Wolbachia (red) are known to infect the oocytes (blue and green) of insects such as Drosophila melanogaster. The bacteria also play a role in targeting parasitic filarial worms, with studies showing that inhibiting Wolbachia's growth can disrupt the worms' survival. The World Mosquito Program in Brazil has been using Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes as a biocontrol strategy. Additionally, citizen science projects are helping to map Wolbachia's presence in various insect species. The article highlights the ongoing research into Wolbachia's antiviral mechanisms and its broader applications in public health. These efforts aim to reduce the spread of diseases by modifying mosquito biology and targeting the microbiome of pathogens.

news.content: Latest Bangladesh Business World Sports Opinion Politics Diplomacy More E-Paper ☀️ 🌐 English বাংলা Russian Hindi Chinese Trending Rangpur Quadruple Murder Mirza Fakhrul Gold Price Tarique Rahman US-Iran Talks × Today's Newspaper Latest World Cup Magazine 2026 Election 2026 Follow Us Print: 25 Aug 2026 Today's Newspaper WORLD MOSQUITO DAY Calls for wider awareness, central oversight amid dengue surge Daily Sun Report, Dhaka Published: 20 Aug 2026, 12:00 AM Updated: 19 Aug 2026, 11:39 PM Share Share options Print Copy link Facebook X WhatsApp Linkedin A A Bangladesh marks World Mosquito Day today amidst an ongoing surge in dengue cases, with public health experts emphasising the need for wider community outreach and stronger institutional coordination. Observed globally every year on 20 August, the day highlights the world’s deadliest animal and the array of vector-borne illnesses it transmits, including dengue, Zika, chikungunya, and yellow fever, which continue to threaten billions worldwide. Yet, as hospital admissions and fatalities from dengue climb daily across Bangladesh, both the Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) and Dhaka North City Corporation (DNCC) have planned no programmes or public engagements to mark the occasion. When contacted, public relations officers from both city bodies confirmed the absence of any official events. DSCC Public Relations Officer Rasel Rahman and DNCC Public Relations Officer Zakir Hossain both conceded that an event should have been scheduled, but confirmed none had been organised. The inaction comes against the backdrop of a steadily worsening dengue crisis. According to Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) data released on Wednesday morning, at least two more patients died and 671 were hospitalised across the country in the 24 hours to 8am on 19 August. The country’s total Dengue toll for the year now stands at 76 deaths and 26,272 hospitalisations. Public health experts and entomologists have criticized the authorities' handling of the vector, noting that despite allocating millions of takas for larvicides and adulticides, city corporations have consistently failed to curb mosquito populations due to acute shortages in technical expertise, logistics, and trained personnel. Dr GM Saifur Rahman, a medical entomologist and associate professor at National University, stressed that World Mosquito Day should serve as a key platform for public health engagement. “This day is directly tied to public safety – mosquitoes affect everyone, and people are dying,” Dr Rahman said. “We should be hosting rallies, discussions, essay competitions, and art events in educational institutions to educate youth and civil society. Crucially, we also need professional, scientific symposia on vector control. Yet, those responsible have made no effort.” Saifur Rahman highlighted fundamental systemic flaws in Bangladesh's vector control apparatus, warning that efforts remain fragmented and reactive. “There is no central body overseeing integrated vector management across the country. City corporations and municipalities operate in isolation. We are now seeing dengue cases emerging from rural union parishads, where there is virtually no manpower or equipment to fight mosquitoes. Nationwide surveillance, vector research, and structured preventive programmes remain virtually non-existent,” he added, calling for meaningful observation of the day to drive evidence-based dengue control and save lives. analysis.event: Bangladesh is experiencing a surge in dengue cases, with public health experts calling for wider awareness and central oversight. The Dhaka city corporations have not organized any events to mark World Mosquito Day, despite the ongoing crisis.

analysis.brief_en: The article reports on a surge in dengue cases in Bangladesh, highlighting the lack of coordinated efforts by city corporations like Dhaka South and North City Corporations to mark World Mosquito Day. According to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), at least two patients died and 671 were hospitalized in the 24 hours leading up to 19 August 2026, bringing the total annual toll to 76 deaths and 26,272 hospitalizations. Public health experts, including Dr. GM Saifur Rahman, criticize the fragmented and reactive approach to vector control, noting acute shortages in technical expertise, logistics, and trained personnel. They emphasize the need for nationwide surveillance, research, and structured preventive programs, as well as central oversight to address the growing crisis. The article underscores the systemic flaws in Bangladesh's dengue management and calls for improved public health engagement to save lives.

news.content: Monday, Aug 24, 2026 Search Hyderabad Telangana AP News India World Entertainment Sport Science and Tech Business Rewind ... NRI View Point cartoon My Space Education Today Reviews Property Lifestyle E-Paper NRI View Point cartoon My Space Reviews Education Today Property Lifestyle Home | Hyderabad | Hyderabad Sees Seasonal Surge In Viral Fevers Flu Like Illnesses Amid Wet Weather Hyderabad sees seasonal surge in viral fevers, flu-like illnesses amid wet weather Persistent wet weather and high humidity have led to a seasonal rise in viral fevers and influenza-like illnesses in Hyderabad. Doctors say symptoms can overlap with dengue and chikungunya, while urging residents to prevent mosquito breeding and avoid self-medication. Exploring Guided Local City Tours By Telangana Today Published Date - 19 August 2026, 05:26 PM Hyderabad: Persistent wet weather and high humidity across Hyderabad have triggered a sharp seasonal surge in viral fevers, influenza-like illnesses (ILI), and suspected vector-borne cases. Outpatient departments across major State-run hospitals, including Fever Hospital, Nallakunta, Gandhi Hospital, Secunderabad, Basthi Dawakhanas, private nursing homes and clinics, are witnessing a surge in patient walk-ins with typical viral fever symptoms. Seasonal health tips According to senior doctors, a majority of patients are reporting overlapping symptoms, which means they are having identical warning symptoms for influenza, common cold, dengue and chikungunya. Powered By VidCrunch Powered by VidCrunch Next Stay Playback speed 1x Normal Quality Auto Back 322p 240p 144p Auto Back 0.25x 0.5x 1x Normal 1.5x 2x 00:00/01:00 The typical symptoms that patients at health care facilities are reporting include sudden high-grade fever, severe body aches and joint pain, extreme fatigue and exhaustion, and headaches. Ordering At-Home Infectious Disease Tests “Wet conditions play a big role in triggering viral fevers during the rainy season. It’s mostly water-borne and vector-borne ailments. Families residing in economically weaker section regions must take precautions from mosquitoes, which are the main culprit for diseases during this time of the year. We are witnessing a slight surge in viral fevers, but the important thing is that families can remain safe by taking simple precautions,” says Superintendent, Fever Hospital, Dr Musa Khan. Doctors have pointed out that prevailing clinical presentation typically includes sudden high-grade fevers, severe body aches (myalgia), extreme fatigue, and respiratory discomfort such as scratchy throats and persistent coughs. While public anxiety frequently centers around dengue during wet spells, doctors made it clear that a large number of patients test negative for dengue and malaria. The real culprits are the aggressive circulating viral and respiratory strains, they added. Managing Chronic Health Conditions Public health authorities have urged residents to remain vigilant against seasonal diseases by getting rid of stagnant water breeding sites, ensuring safe drinking water, and avoiding self-medication. analysis.event: Hyderabad is experiencing a seasonal surge in viral fevers and flu-like illnesses, which are attributed to persistent wet weather and high humidity. Doctors have noted overlapping symptoms with dengue and chikungunya, but the exact cause is not confirmed. The event is reported by Telangana Today.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Outpatient departments in major hospitals and clinics in Hyderabad are witnessing a surge in patient walk-ins with typical viral fever symptoms. The health authorities have emphasized the need for vigilance against seasonal diseases, but no specific case or death counts are provided. The risk is associated with the spread of vector-borne diseases, though the exact risk level is not explicitly stated.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Public health authorities have urged residents to take precautions such as eliminating stagnant water breeding sites, ensuring safe drinking water, and avoiding self-medication. However, the situation remains under investigation, and the exact nature of the outbreak is not fully confirmed.

news.wechat_summary_zh: 时间：持续降雨和高湿度导致海得拉巴在雨季出现病毒热及流感样疾病的季节性上升。相关情况已于2026年8月19日发布。；地点与对象：此次事件发生在印度海得拉巴(特伦甘纳邦)，涉及普通人群，特别是经济弱势家庭，当局敦促其采取措施预防蚊媒孳生。；事件：海得拉巴正经历病毒热及流感样疾病的季节性激增，主要归因于持续降雨和高湿度。医生指出其症状与登革热及基孔肯雅热存在重叠，但具体病因尚未确认。相关情况由《Telangana Today》报道。；影响与风险：海得拉巴主要医院及诊所门诊部接诊量激增，患者多表现出典型病毒热症状。卫生当局强调需警惕季节性疾病，但未提供具体病例或死亡人数。风险与媒介媒介传播疾病的传播相关，但未明确说明具体风险等级。；应对与不确定性：公共卫生当局已敦促居民采取预防措施，包括清除积水孳生地、确保饮用水安全及避免自行用药。然而，当前疫情仍在调查中，具体暴发病原体尚未完全确认。

Risk Can Continue Beyond Monsoon, Doctors Warn Telangana Deepika Pasham 20 August 2026 5:22 PM20 August 2026 5:22 PM Internal medicine specialist Dr Sudhir B.S. said changing weather conditions and poor water management were creating mosquito breeding sites throughout the year. x In cities, even small amounts of stagnant water in coolers, flowerpots, open containers, construction sites and terraces can provide breeding grounds.(File Photo) Select Deccan Chronicle Now Hyderabad: Mosquito-borne diseases such as dengue, malaria and chikungunya are no longer confined to the monsoon season, with changing weather patterns, rising temperatures, irregular rainfall and rapid urbanisation allowing mosquitoes to breed for longer periods, doctors said on the occasion of the World Mosquito Day. Senior general physician Dr Syed Mustafa Ashraf said mosquito-borne infections were increasingly being seen outside the traditional seasonal pattern. In cities, even small amounts of stagnant water in coolers, flowerpots, open containers, construction sites and terraces can provide breeding grounds. Also Read - Call For 75 Per Cent Reservations In Jobs For Adivasis Of Agency Areas In Police Recruitment Advertisement “Mosquito control cannot be limited to the monsoon. Prevention has to continue throughout the year,” he said, stressing the need to remove stagnant water, cover water containers and use measures to prevent mosquito bites. Senior consultant, general medicine, Dr Chaitanya Challa said one of the major concerns was that people often dismiss fever outside the monsoon as a routine viral infection. Dengue, malaria and chikungunya can initially cause similar symptoms such as fever, headache, body pain, weakness, nausea and vomiting. Also Read - Hyd-Based Tech Start-Up Water Raises $2.5 Million “Persistent fever, repeated vomiting, abdominal pain, unusual bleeding, excessive weakness, drowsiness or breathing difficulty should not be ignored,” he said. He cautioned that in dengue, a fall in temperature does not always mean that the patient is recovering. The critical phase can occur around the time the fever settles, usually during days three to seven of illness and some patients can develop complications during this period. Also Read - Special Drive To Complete 16.06 Saplings Planting From Today Discover more Implementing Enterprise AI And Machine Learning Tools E-paper subscription OTT Platform Guide Senior consultant-general physician Dr Krishna Murthy Daram said the risk of mosquito-borne diseases depended on local temperature, rainfall, humidity, mosquito activity and environmental conditions rather than simply the calendar season. Internal medicine specialist Dr Sudhir B.S. said changing weather conditions and poor water management were creating mosquito breeding sites throughout the year.
